name: Executive Leadership & Future Readiness Framework
recommended: 5 core competencies plus 2-3 role-specific ones (7-8 in total)

clusters.name: Lead the Future
clusters.description: Vision and foresight: seeing what is coming and positioning the organization ahead of it.

clusters.name: Lead the Business
clusters.description: Transformation and AI: changing how the business works and delivering value from it.

clusters.name: Lead People & the Organization
clusters.description: People and organization: building the teams, culture and relationships the future requires.

clusters.name: Lead Self
clusters.description: Self-leadership: the foundation for leading others through constant change.

scale.Limited: Limited or inconsistent evidence. Behaviors appear only when prompted; impact is mostly personal.
scale.Borderline: Some evidence. Applies the competency in familiar situations; impact is visible within their own team.
scale.Solid: Consistent evidence. Applies it reliably and proactively; measurable impact across their function.
scale.Outstanding: Strong, sustained evidence. Shapes how others work; impact across the enterprise or industry; others learn from them.
scale.N/A: Insufficient evidence. Not enough evidence to rate. Name what is missing.

N-1 executive.level3: Executes and scales the C-level agenda in their area
N-1 executive.evidence: Function KPIs, team metrics, initiatives delivered

C-level.scope: The whole enterprise and its ecosystem
C-level.level3: Sets direction, investment priorities and culture for the organization
C-level.evidence: Enterprise KPIs, board and investor feedback, market position

competencies.name: Strategic Foresight & Scenario Thinking
competencies.definition: Anticipates disruption from technology, markets, regulation and geopolitics, and turns it into strategic options.
competencies.evidence: one scenario or foresight exercise that shaped a strategic decision, investment or risk response.

rubric.Limited: Focuses on the current year; reacts to change after it happens.
rubric.Borderline: Follows major trends; occasionally discusses their impact but rarely acts on them.
rubric.Solid: Regularly scans trends, builds 2–3 scenarios for their area and adjusts plans and investments accordingly.
rubric.Outstanding: Shapes enterprise strategy through foresight; spots disruptions early and positions the company ahead of competitors.

questions: Which trend will most change your industry in the next 3–5 years, and what have you done about it already?
Tell me about a time you acted on an early signal before others did.

competencies.name: Thought Leadership & External Voice
competencies.definition: Shapes the conversation in their industry and positions the company as a forward-thinking leader.
areas: a clear, distinctive point of view
external visibility (conferences, LinkedIn, media, industry bodies)
bringing outside insights back into the organization
competencies.evidence: a defined thought-leadership agenda plus 2–4 external contributions (keynote, article, panel, podcast) with reach or engagement data.

rubric.Limited: Little external presence; no clear point of view beyond their role.
rubric.Borderline: Occasional external activity, mostly reactive or generic content.
rubric.Solid: A clear point of view on the future of their domain; contributes externally several times a year; brings insights back to the team.
rubric.Outstanding: A recognized industry voice; sets the agenda in their field; attracts talent, clients and partners to the company.

questions: What do you believe about the future of your field that most peers don't?
How has your external voice created value for your organization?

competencies.name: Customer & Value Obsession
competencies.definition: Anchors decisions in customer value and future market needs.
competencies.evidence: improvement in customer KPIs (NPS, retention, time-to-value) or a new offer shaped by customer insight.

rubric.Limited: Decisions are driven by internal priorities; limited direct customer contact.
rubric.Borderline: Considers customer feedback when it is presented; customer metrics are tracked but rarely drive action.
rubric.Solid: Spends regular time with customers; uses customer data and AI insights to shape priorities; improves customer KPIs.
rubric.Outstanding: Anticipates needs customers have not expressed; creates new value propositions or business models; builds a customer-first culture.

questions: When did you last change a major decision because of customer insight?
How do you anticipate needs customers can't yet articulate?

competencies.name: Sustainability & Purpose-Led Leadership
competencies.definition: Integrates long-term environmental, social and governance value into strategy and execution.
areas: ESG and CSRD-related targets for their scope
connecting the team to the company's purpose
competencies.evidence: ESG targets met for their scope plus one sustainability-driven business improvement.

rubric.Limited: Treats sustainability as a compliance topic owned by others.
rubric.Borderline: Meets required ESG targets; purpose is mentioned but not linked to daily decisions.
rubric.Solid: Embeds ESG targets in plans; finds business value in sustainability; team understands how their work links to purpose.
rubric.Outstanding: Makes sustainability a competitive advantage; shapes the enterprise ESG strategy; recognized externally for purpose-led leadership.

questions: Give an example where sustainability created business value, not only cost.
How do you connect your team to the company's purpose?

competencies.name: AI Fluency & Agentic Ways of Working
competencies.definition: Leads by example and creates the conditions for the team to use AI confidently and responsibly.
areas: own use of AI in executive work (decision prep, analysis, board communication)
understanding what AI agents can and cannot do
competencies.evidence: one recurring AI or agentic use case in their own work plus measurable team adoption (e.g., % of team actively using approved tools, upskilling completed).

rubric.Limited: Rarely uses AI personally; delegates AI topics to IT or specialists.
rubric.Borderline: Uses AI for occasional tasks; supports team adoption when asked.
rubric.Solid: Uses AI and agents routinely in their own work; actively drives team adoption and upskilling; sets clear guardrails.
rubric.Outstanding: Visible AI champion; shapes enterprise AI ambition; their area is a benchmark for adoption that others copy.

questions: Walk me through how you personally used AI in your work this week.
How have you increased AI adoption in your team, and how do you measure it?

competencies.name: AI-Driven Problem Solving & Workflow Redesign
competencies.definition: Redesigns workflows and the operating model of their function to create business value with AI.
areas: selecting high-value use cases tied to C-level priorities
tracking ROI and scaling or stopping pilots
competencies.evidence: one function-level AI initiative with measurable business impact (cost, cycle time, quality, revenue or customer), reported to the C-level sponsor, with a documented scale-or-stop decision.

rubric.Limited: AI is used to automate isolated tasks; no link to business outcomes.
rubric.Borderline: Runs AI pilots, but few reach scale or show measured ROI.
rubric.Solid: Redesigns end-to-end workflows with AI; delivers measurable impact; scales what works and stops what doesn't.
rubric.Outstanding: Reinvents the operating or business model with AI; creates new sources of value; sets the enterprise playbook.

questions: Describe a workflow you redesigned with AI. What was the before and after in numbers?
Tell me about an AI pilot you stopped, and why.

competencies.name: Transformation & Change Leadership
competencies.definition: Leads people through continuous change and ambiguity while sustaining performance.
areas: pacing change to the organization's capacity
maintaining engagement and results during change
competencies.evidence: a transformation milestone delivered, with engagement or adoption metrics held or improved.

rubric.Limited: Implements change top-down; resistance and drops in performance are common.
rubric.Borderline: Communicates change but struggles to sustain momentum or engagement.
rubric.Solid: Builds a compelling case for change; involves people early; delivers milestones while keeping engagement stable.
rubric.Outstanding: Makes the organization change-ready as a permanent capability; leads enterprise-wide transformations successfully.

questions: Tell me about the hardest transformation you led. What resistance did you face and how did you handle it?
How do you know when the organization is at its change capacity?

competencies.name: Decisive Judgment Under Uncertainty
competencies.definition: Makes timely, sound decisions with incomplete information, combining data, AI insight and experience.
areas: use of data and AI to inform judgment
competencies.evidence: key decisions documented with their rationale plus at least one example of a fast pivot or a decision to stop something.

rubric.Limited: Delays decisions waiting for certainty, or decides on intuition alone.
rubric.Borderline: Makes sound decisions in familiar situations; hesitates under ambiguity.
rubric.Solid: Decides at the right speed with incomplete data; uses data and AI well; adjusts quickly when facts change.
rubric.Outstanding: Trusted for high-stakes calls; builds a decision culture of speed, accountability and learning across the organization.

questions: Describe a major decision you made with incomplete information. What did you do when it turned out partly wrong?

competencies.name: Digital, Cyber & Business Resilience
competencies.definition: Keeps the business robust against shocks: cyber, supply chain, geopolitical and technological.
areas: treating risk as a strategic topic
competencies.evidence: a resilience or crisis plan tested (simulation or tabletop exercise), with gaps closed.

rubric.Limited: Sees resilience and cyber as IT or risk topics; no continuity plan for their area.
rubric.Borderline: Has plans on paper but they are rarely tested.
rubric.Solid: Tests plans regularly; understands key cyber and operational risks; leads calmly through incidents.
rubric.Outstanding: Builds resilience into strategy and design; turns crises into opportunities; sets the enterprise standard.

questions: Tell me about a crisis you led through.
What would you do in the first 24 hours of a major cyber incident affecting your area?

competencies.name: Ecosystem & Partnership Orchestration
competencies.definition: Creates value beyond the organization's own boundaries through partners, startups, academia and platforms.
areas: using external capabilities instead of building everything in-house
competencies.evidence: one partnership or co-innovation initiative launched or scaled, with defined value.

rubric.Limited: Works mainly inside the organization; partners are treated as suppliers.
rubric.Solid: Actively builds partnerships that create measurable value; uses the ecosystem to accelerate innovation.
rubric.Outstanding: Orchestrates an ecosystem that creates a competitive advantage; the company is a partner of choice.

questions: Which partnership created the most value in your career, and how did you build it?
When do you choose to partner rather than build?

competencies.name: People Leadership & Talent Multiplication
competencies.definition: Inspires, empowers and grows leaders, making the team stronger than the sum of its parts.
competencies.evidence: team engagement score, regretted attrition, ready-now successors for key roles, and at least one leader promoted or grown.

rubric.Limited: Directs and controls; team depends on them for decisions; high regretted attrition.
rubric.Borderline: Supports the team and gives feedback, but delegates little; succession is thin.
rubric.Solid: Sets clear direction, empowers and coaches; strong engagement; ready successors for key roles.
rubric.Outstanding: Known as a builder of leaders; their people are promoted across the company; attracts top talent.

questions: Name two leaders you developed. Where are they now, and what was your role?
How do you create psychological safety in a high-performance team?

competencies.name: Culture & Inclusive Leadership
competencies.definition: Builds an inclusive, high-trust, high-performance culture fit for constant change.
areas: giving diverse perspectives a real voice
addressing behaviors that undermine the culture
competencies.evidence: inclusion and culture pulse results plus one concrete culture initiative led personally.

rubric.Limited: Culture is not a priority; tolerates behaviors that conflict with the values.
rubric.Borderline: Supports culture and inclusion initiatives but rarely leads them.
rubric.Solid: Role-models the values; actively seeks diverse views; addresses poor behavior promptly; culture scores improve.
rubric.Outstanding: Shapes the enterprise culture; their area is a benchmark for inclusion and trust.

questions: Tell me about a time you challenged a behavior that conflicted with your values.
How do you make sure quieter or different voices shape your decisions?

competencies.name: Human + AI Workforce Design
competencies.definition: Shapes the future workforce: roles, skills and human–AI collaboration.
areas: strategic workforce planning for future capabilities
competencies.evidence: a future-skills plan for their organization, with reskilling progress and at least one role redesigned.

rubric.Limited: Plans headcount on today's roles; no view of how AI changes the work.
rubric.Borderline: Aware of AI's impact on roles; reskilling is ad hoc.
rubric.Solid: Has mapped AI's impact on roles; runs a reskilling plan; redesigns roles for human–AI collaboration.
rubric.Outstanding: Defines the enterprise future-of-work strategy; transitions people responsibly and at scale.

questions: How will AI change the roles in your team over the next 2–3 years? What have you already done to prepare your people?

competencies.name: Enterprise Mindset & Systems Thinking
competencies.definition: Optimizes for the whole company, not only their own function.
areas: making trade-offs in the enterprise interest
competencies.evidence: one cross-functional initiative co-led, with shared outcomes and feedback from C-suite peers.

rubric.Limited: Protects their own area; decisions create problems elsewhere.
rubric.Borderline: Collaborates with peers when needed; trade-offs mostly favor their own function.
rubric.Solid: Considers enterprise impact in decisions; co-leads cross-functional work; shares resources when it helps the company.
rubric.Outstanding: Acts as an enterprise leader first; breaks down silos; trusted by peers to represent the whole company.

questions: Tell me about a time you gave up something for your function to benefit the company.
How do you work with peers whose priorities conflict with yours?

competencies.name: Stakeholder & Board Influence
competencies.definition: Builds trust and alignment with the board, investors, regulators, unions and partners.
competencies.evidence: key stakeholder outcomes achieved (approvals, alliances, agreements) plus feedback from the board or CEO.

rubric.Limited: Communicates mainly within their own area; struggles with senior or external audiences.
rubric.Borderline: Presents clearly to senior audiences; influence depends on formal authority.
rubric.Solid: Builds trust with the board and external stakeholders; secures approvals; handles conflicting interests well.
rubric.Outstanding: A trusted voice with the board and key stakeholders; shapes decisions well beyond their formal role.

questions: Describe a time you won board or investor support for a difficult proposal.
How did you handle a stakeholder whose interests conflicted with yours?

competencies.name: Trust, Ethics & Responsible AI Governance
competencies.definition: Keeps innovation safe, compliant and trusted by customers, employees and regulators.
areas: applying the EU AI Act and data privacy rules (GDPR)
transparency and human oversight of AI decisions
competencies.evidence: an AI and data risk review completed for their area, with no unmanaged critical risks.

rubric.Limited: Sees ethics and compliance as slowing things down; limited awareness of AI risks.
rubric.Borderline: Follows the rules when reminded; reacts to issues after they occur.
rubric.Solid: Builds guardrails in from the start; knows the key regulations; ensures human oversight; escalates risks early.
rubric.Outstanding: Shapes enterprise AI governance; makes trust a competitive advantage; balances innovation and responsibility.

questions: Tell me about a time you stopped or changed an initiative for ethical or compliance reasons.
How do you make sure AI decisions in your area remain explainable and overseen by people?

competencies.name: Self-Mastery & Continuous Growth
competencies.definition: Leads themselves well: self-aware, resilient and continuously improving.
areas: awareness of their own blind spots
competencies.evidence: a personal development plan with 2–3 goals achieved, 360° feedback showing visible progress, and one habit they changed or stopped.

rubric.Limited: Rarely seeks feedback; reacts defensively; little investment in their own learning; shows strain under pressure.
rubric.Borderline: Accepts feedback and has a development plan, but follow-through is inconsistent.
rubric.Solid: Actively seeks feedback and acts on it; learns continuously; manages energy well; stays composed under pressure.
rubric.Outstanding: Models vulnerability and growth openly; reinvents their own leadership as the context changes; creates a learning culture around them.
